content.p: Kirstin Blaise Lobato was convicted twice of the 2001 killing of a homeless man in Las Vegas, and she was later exonerated. Nevada courts vacated her convictions in December 2017, prosecutors dropped the case, and she walked out of custody in January 2018 after nearly 16 years in prison. In December 2024 a federal jury found that two Las Vegas police detectives had fabricated evidence against her and awarded her more than $34 million. In October 2026 Nevada television and press reported that the dispute had ended in a $29.5 million settlement with the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department.
The man she was convicted of killing was Duran Bailey. The reporting on the 2026 settlement does not name anyone else as his killer.

KTNV in Las Vegas reported on 6 October 2026 that Lobato had reached a $29.5 million settlement with the police department. The station said the figure appeared on the 9 September agenda of the Metropolitan Police Committee on Fiscal Affairs and that the deal was reached "last month". It also said the department had appealed after the 2024 verdict. Hoodline, citing the Las Vegas Review-Journal, reported that the appeal had been resolved through mediation and that Lobato received the whole settlement amount.

Her lawyer, David Owens, told KTNV that the settlement ended litigation that "could have continued for years further". According to Hoodline, he said the deal guaranteed quick payment, because an appeal could have delayed it, and that the judgment had been gathering interest since the verdict. He also said the size of the payment reflected the strength of her case. "Blaise had her day in court, the jury heard what she had to say and sided with her and now, she can go on and move on with her life," Owens said, as quoted by Hoodline. The police department did not respond to KTNV's request for comment, and KTNV noted that its usual policy is not to comment on litigation. Hoodline, citing the Review-Journal, said the department did not respond to a request there either.
It has not been reported whether the detectives' own motions for a new trial and for judgment as a matter of law, filed in February 2025, were ever decided.
content.h2: A rumour, a visit to Panaca and an arrest
content.p: Lobato grew up in Panaca, a small town that the Innocence Project and KTNV describe as about three hours from Las Vegas. According to the Innocence Project, in late May 2001 she was visiting friends in Las Vegas when a man tried to rape her in a motel parking lot. She carried a small knife, slashed at the man's groin and got away. She told friends and family about it over the following weeks.

On 8 July 2001 Bailey was found dead in Las Vegas. The Innocence Project said Bailey's body was found next to a dumpster at around 10 p.m. The Las Vegas Sun placed it near a bank dumpster on West Flamingo Road. CNN and KTNV reported that he had been homeless and had a slashed neck, a cracked skull and mutilation injuries.

On 20 July, according to the Innocence Project, detectives received a call from a Panaca resident who had heard from another resident that Lobato had cut off a man's penis in Las Vegas. Detectives drove to her family home. Lobato later told TODAY that she assumed they were homicide detectives because the man who attacked her must have died. The Innocence Project says she recorded a statement that placed the attack in a motel parking lot, said it had happened "at least a month ago" and described a man who was alive and moving when she left. She expressed remorse, the group says, and the detective took her remarks as a confession. The Innocence Project says the police had no physical or forensic evidence linking her to the crime.

The police account differed. AP and CNN reported that police maintained she had told someone in jail that she killed a man who tried to rape her while on a three-day methamphetamine binge. Lobato said she had never met Bailey.

At her first trial in 2002, prosecutors argued that she had killed Bailey in the early hours of 8 July and driven home to Panaca. The Las Vegas Sun reported that prosecutors pointed to cell phone bills, said she had left Panaca on 6 July after arguing with her parents and said she returned in the early hours of 8 July. Defence lawyers called witnesses who said she was in Panaca from 2 July to 9 July, according to the same report. The Innocence Project said the prosecution accepted in its closing argument that Lobato was in Panaca by 11:30 a.m. on 8 July. The prosecution leaned on the medical examiner, who put Bailey's death as much as 24 hours before the 3:50 a.m. pronouncement on 9 July.

The jury convicted her of first-degree murder. On 27 August 2002, Judge Valorie Vega sentenced her to 40 to 100 years in prison, and ordered a concurrent term of five to 15 years on a second charge relating to Bailey's body. Lobato had agreed to the 40-to-100 range after the conviction so that a jury could not impose a life term without parole, the Las Vegas Sun reported.

In 2004 the Nevada Supreme Court threw out that verdict and sentence because her lawyers had not been allowed to cross-examine a prosecution witness who testified that Lobato confessed in jail, AP reported. A second trial in 2006 ended in convictions for voluntary manslaughter, mutilation and weapon charges. CNN and KTNV give the sentence as 13 to 45 years; Fox5 Vegas printed 13 to 35.

The Intercept, in a 2017 account, wrote that the medical examiner who had first given an estimate that would have all but cleared Lobato widened his window by the time of the 2006 trial. The Intercept said he later told its reporters that his first estimate was his best.
content.h2: The flies that were not there
content.p: In November 2016 the Nevada Supreme Court ordered a hearing, finding that her alibi evidence was strong and that the time of death was crucial, according to The Intercept. The Innocence Project and the Las Vegas lawyers David Chesnoff and Richard Schonfeld took up her case, KTNV reported.

The hearing in Judge Stefany Miley's court in October 2017 turned on insects. The Review-Journal reported that four forensic experts for the defence testified that Bailey probably died at about 9 p.m. on 8 July, when Lobato was seen in Panaca, a conclusion they based on the absence of blowfly egg colonies in the photographs and reports. A forensic pathologist, the Innocence Project said, reached a similar view from rigor mortis changes. The Intercept reported that the prosecutor, Sandra DiGiacomo, argued that local blowflies had not been studied and called two witnesses.

On 19 December 2017 Miley vacated the convictions. The Innocence Project said she found that Lobato's trial lawyers were ineffective for failing to call pathology and entomology experts. On 29 December, Chief Judge Elizabeth Gonzalez dismissed all charges after prosecutors declined to hold a third trial.

The prosecution did not concede innocence. Chief Deputy District Attorney Sandra DiGiacomo told the court, "Although we fully believe in her guilt, as did the 24 members of our community who found her guilty beyond a reasonable doubt, our resources are such that we are electing not to proceed with the third trial of this defendant," the Review-Journal reported. The Review-Journal reported that an unrelated 2007 conviction had added a year to her sentence, to be served after the killing sentence, and that Potkin said she would push for immediate release. Lobato was released on 3 January 2018, according to the Innocence Project and TODAY.
"I don't think I can get those years back," Lobato told KTNV in 2018. "All I can do is move forward."

The Innocence Project said police did not investigate other people who had a motive. It reported that on 1 July 2001 Bailey attacked a woman who lived in the building beside the bank where his body was later found, and who it says he threatened. She reported it to police on 5 July, it said, and told male neighbours who had a continuing dispute with him. KTNV said court records described that dispute. The Innocence Project says police dismissed these possible suspects too early. The reporting does not say that any of them has been charged.
content.h2: The certificate of innocence and the civil suit
content.p: A state court issued Lobato a certificate of innocence in October 2023, according to CNN and Hoodline. The Clark County sheriff, Kevin McMahill, and the district attorney, Steve Wolfson, challenged how her lawyers obtained it, asking Attorney General Aaron Ford to investigate, CNN reported. Hoodline said Lobato had settled a separate state innocence claim with Ford's office, which drew pushback from the two officials.

Her federal suit, filed in 2019 against the police department, alleged fabrication of evidence and intentional infliction of emotional distress, KLAS reported. Her lawyers argued that the detectives misrepresented her statements about the earlier attack and wrote false reports suggesting that she had confessed, according to Loevy and Loevy. The trial began on 2 December 2024 and lasted ten days, KLAS said. CNN reported that the department had agreed beforehand to pay damages if the jury ruled for Lobato.

On Thursday 12 December 2024 the jury found that the department and two retired detectives, Thomas Thowsen and James LaRochelle, had fabricated evidence and intentionally inflicted emotional distress. According to CNN, the award was $34 million in compensatory damages, to be paid by the department, plus $10,000 in punitive damages against each detective. Lobato, then 41, said after the verdict that she had "no idea what the rest of my life is going to look like". Her attorney Elizabeth Wang said, "Of course they intentionally framed her". Her lawyers described the award as believed to be the largest to a wrongfully convicted woman in US history.

The detectives' lawyer, Craig Anderson, said an appeal was likely. On 3 February 2025 he filed a motion for a new trial, arguing among other things that the judge's evidentiary rulings had violated his clients' rights and that the weight of the evidence went against the verdict. He also moved for judgment as a matter of law. On the same day Lobato asked for interest on the award. The settlement reported in October 2026 followed those filings.
